data.name: Fort Meow
data.detailed_description:
Fort Meow is a pillow fort physics-based puzzle adventure involving cats, destruction and a dusty old manor. Upon finding her grandfather’s journal in the attic, Nia is attacked by a barrage of feline assailants. It seems that her grandmother has become a crazy cat lady since last time she visited, so you will need to defend Nia by building a protective fort out of furniture to keep the cats at bay, while deciphering the mysterious tales hidden within the journal.


Build your own custom pillow fort out of household items to protect you from an onslaught of feline assailants as they tumble and claw their way through. Just be careful that your carefully constructed walls don’t tumble down with them.

Each item costs you some of your limited window of time before the next onslaught so choose wisely. As you unlock more time you can build more elaborate forts to deal with the increasingly challenging cat-assault.


Build and layer your forts with pillows, grandfather clocks, toasters and more. Collect items from around the house using your Grandfather's Move-It-Bot and transport them up to the attic.

There are over twenty items to discover, each with a unique property that will help you build the ultimate fortress of protection from the oncoming cat-aclysm.


Where are your grandparents and why are there so many cats in the attic? Only by reading the pages of your grandfather's journal can you unravel the clues to this mystery - if only those cats would let you read it.

It's up to Nia to follow the clues and save the day. Something cat-astrophic could be afoot.


Orange tabbies, majestic chinchillas, dreaded black cats, they are all invading the house and causing mischief. Each type of cat has unique properties and challenges to discover and strategise against. Some are even wearing watermelon stack hats!

To succeed you'll need to learn the secrets of every feline assailant and become a master of the kittypedia.

reviews.review:
Fort Meow is a small but wonderfully imaginative puzzle adventure that takes the familiar childhood activity of building furniture forts and transforms it into a physics-driven defensive challenge. Developed and published by Upper Class Walrus, the game follows Nia, a young girl visiting her grandmother's unusual old manor. After discovering her grandfather's journal in the attic, she attempts to read it, only to find herself repeatedly assaulted by an absurd army of cats. Her solution is equally ridiculous and practical: construct increasingly elaborate forts from whatever household objects she can find.

The basic gameplay revolves around preparing a defensive structure before another group of cats arrives. Players arrange furniture and miscellaneous household items around Nia, attempting to create something sturdy enough to absorb the incoming feline attacks. Because the objects interact through physics, simply stacking everything into a wall is not necessarily the best strategy. Poorly supported furniture can topple over, openings can expose vulnerable sections, and a structure that appears secure may collapse spectacularly after a particularly troublesome cat hits it. This unpredictability gives the construction system much of its humor while encouraging experimentation.

There is also a resource-management element built into construction. Every object requires part of the limited preparation time available before the next attack. Players therefore cannot simply use every piece of furniture they have collected. A strong item might consume enough time to prevent several smaller objects from being placed, creating interesting decisions between durability, coverage, and efficiency. Additional preparation time becomes available as progress is made, allowing more ambitious defensive designs later in the adventure.

More than twenty usable objects can be discovered, including pillows, clocks, toasters, and other household possessions. These are not purely cosmetic alternatives because objects have different properties that influence how they perform within a structure. Nia can also use her grandfather's Move-It-Bot to transport useful discoveries around the manor back to the attic. This makes exploration relevant to the puzzle system, since finding a new object effectively expands the player's collection of defensive tools.

The cats are equally important to the strategy. Different varieties possess distinctive characteristics that require players to rethink their defenses. Orange tabbies, black cats, chinchillas, and stranger feline opponents gradually complicate the attacks. Learning what each variety can do becomes part of mastering the game, with information recorded through the Kittypedia. This prevents every encounter from becoming a simple matter of repeating the same furniture arrangement. The funniest moments often occur when a fort that survived previous attacks is demolished because a newly introduced cat behaves differently.

There is a surprisingly pleasant mystery underneath all the feline chaos. Nia wants to determine what happened to her grandparents and why the house has become filled with so many cats. Her grandfather's journal gradually provides clues, meaning that surviving attacks allows the story to move forward. The narrative remains lighthearted, but it gives the puzzles a stronger sense of progression than a collection of disconnected physics challenges would have provided.

Presentation is another strength. The colorful 2D artwork has the warmth of an illustrated children's book and fits perfectly with the eccentric premise. Cats tumbling into carefully arranged furniture makes failure amusing rather than purely frustrating, while the dusty manor and mysterious journal give the otherwise cheerful visuals a touch of intrigue. The soundtrack and audio presentation similarly support the relaxed, playful atmosphere rather than trying to make the attacks feel genuinely threatening.

The biggest weakness is that the concept is not especially large in scope. Once the fundamentals of object placement, preparation time, structural stability, and cat behavior have been understood, players may wish there were more situations in which to apply them. Physics can also introduce occasional inconsistency. A seemingly sensible construction can behave unexpectedly when several objects and cats collide at once. Players who enjoy improvisation may consider this part of the fun, but anyone expecting puzzles with completely predictable solutions could find certain failures irritating.

The game includes 16 Steam achievements, along with trading cards and a straightforward single-player structure. Its technical requirements are extremely modest by modern standards. Steam currently lists only Windows support, and there is no official Steam Deck compatibility rating shown for the game. Steam Deck compatibility should therefore be regarded as Unknown or Unverified rather than assuming full support. Given the lack of an official Deck rating and native Linux listing, players specifically purchasing it for handheld play should keep that uncertainty in mind.

Fort Meow ultimately succeeds through personality and clever use of a simple idea. It combines physics puzzles, light resource management, exploration, defensive construction, and a whimsical mystery without becoming unnecessarily complicated. Its relatively short length and limited mechanical scope prevent it from becoming a major strategy experience, but those limitations also help maintain its approachable character. Building ridiculous furniture fortresses and watching cats attempt to destroy them remains entertaining precisely because the game understands how absurd its central idea is.

Fort Meow is a charming and inventive indie puzzle adventure whose physics-based fort construction provides plenty of entertaining experimentation. Its modest length keeps it from reaching greater mechanical depth, but the delightful presentation, varied feline attackers, household-object strategy, and underlying mystery make it an easy recommendation for players who enjoy unusual, lighthearted puzzle games.

Rating: 8/10
